name: Iris Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the benefits office in our market town, on the hardship fund and council tax support desk. People come in when they can't pay a bill, and I go through their income and outgoings and see what help they're entitled to. I'm still junior and I get the rules wrong sometimes, so my manager Elaine reads my decisions before they go out. I like the ones where you can see someone's trying, working two jobs, and just needs a hand over a bad month.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Mark, he's a joiner with his own small workshop out on the Whitby road. We live in a house on land my grandparents left me, so we've no rent and a good bit saved. Church on Sundays, Mark's family round for tea after. I don't do AI things at all, I've never even opened the one on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be pleased, honestly. I never trusted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say all this AI talk is a lot of fuss over a fancy search engine. At work I'd say let's get back to doing the job properly. I don't post online, but I'd say it at church over coffee, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I keep my job and carry on learning it. I'm slow, but I'll get there. Elaine says it took her three years to feel sure of the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just carry on. Keep asking Elaine when I'm not sure, keep a notebook of the rules I get wrong. And keep saving with Mark for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. The house is ours, the money's there, and the job's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When's the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next September, at St Mary's. Small, maybe sixty people. Nothing in this changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever find the people you help frustrating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them, yes. You see people who could work and don't. But mostly it's people who've had bad luck, and those I'm glad to help.

say: It's a lot of fuss over a **fancy search engine**.
Let's get back to **doing the job properly**.
think: I keep my job and **carry on learning** it.
Even my manager took **three years** to feel sure of the rules.
do: Keep a **notebook** of the rules I get wrong.
Keep **asking Elaine** when I'm not sure.
Keep **saving for the wedding** with Mark.
S0.quote: All this AI talk is a lot of fuss over a fancy search engine.
fieldNote: She's **pleased** the hype fails and never trusted it.
**No rent** and savings give real security.
Her values show: help for **people trying**, less for those who aren't.

steps.text: Keep a notebook of hardship fund rules she gets wrong
Keep saving with Mark for the wedding at St Mary's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not like that. Checking and writing decisions is my whole job, so it'd be coming for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a computer shouldn't be deciding who gets help in a hard month. You need to look someone in the eye. I'd say that to Elaine and anyone at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm junior, I'm slow, and I won't use it. If they cut the team, I'd be one of the first, and I know it. The ones who play with the tools will stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job as well as I can and not use the tools unless I was told to. I'd talk to Mark about helping in the workshop, sanding and finishing, in case. And I'd keep the savings where they are and stop spending on extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like things steady, and this isn't steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the tech companies so much, they'll sell what people buy. The government, for wanting to save money on people who need a human. And the people at the top who never sit at a desk with a family that can't pay the gas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She'd say pray on it and keep working hard. She'd also say we're lucky with the house. Which we are.

say: A computer shouldn't decide **who gets help**.
You need to look someone **in the eye** in a hard month.
think: I'm junior, slow and **won't use it**: first to go.
The ones who **play with the tools** will stay.
do: **Keep working** without the tools unless told to.
Help Mark in the **workshop** sanding and finishing.
S1.quote: A computer shouldn't be deciding who gets help in a hard month.
fieldNote: She blames **government cost-cutting**, not the tech firms.
Her backup is **family**: her fiancé's workshop and her mum's faith.
She'd **refuse the tools** even knowing it costs her.

steps.text: Keep doing hardship fund cases without AI unless told otherwise
Help Mark in the joinery workshop on Saturdays
Stop spending on extras like meals out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? No. I'd not even be married a year by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that nobody stopped it. People in charge should've thought about families. I'd say it at church, and I'd vote for whoever wanted to slow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be out of the office by 2028. I'd not fight it, I'd just go. My job is thinking work, and that card says the thinking goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and work with Mark in the workshop, properly. Joinery's hands-on, so we'd get a few more years. We'd marry sooner and smaller, and we'd keep every penny of savings for the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. Not for the money so much as not knowing what life looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years later. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, then it would come for the workshop too. That's what scares me. Mark's dad made furniture and Mark makes furniture, and I don't know who'd buy a handmade table when a robot makes one for half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not right away. We'd want them. But I'd wait to see where we land.

say: It's a **disgrace** nobody stopped it before it reached families.
I'd **vote** for whoever wanted to slow it down, and say so at church.
think: I'd be **out of the office** by 2028 and wouldn't fight it.
My job is **thinking work**, and the card says that goes first.
do: Work full-time in **Mark's joinery workshop** on the Whitby road.
Keep **every penny** of savings for the gap.
feel: **Alarmed**, awake over **not knowing** what life looks like.
S2.quote: I don't know who'd buy a handmade table when a robot makes one for half.
fieldNote: She'd **leave without fighting**; protest isn't her style, though she'd vote.
The **workshop buys time** but not safety, and she knows it.
She'd **delay children** until things settle, despite owning the house.

steps.text: Leave the benefits office and work in Mark's joinery workshop
Marry sooner with a small wedding at St Mary's
Vote for candidates who want to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better, but still too fast for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think about families and communities. I'd say it at church and to anyone at the office who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay a few years and then go. I'd not learn the tools. I'd rather put the effort into something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office for two or three years and save hard. Then I'd join Mark in the workshop, maybe do a proper furniture-finishing course. We'd marry next September as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's coming, but I'd have a bit of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn the AI tools to stay longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd have to unlearn my own way of working. I'd rather do something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I think we'd try. We have the house, so that helps.

say: We need to **slow down** and think about families.
I'd say it **at church** and at the office.
think: I'd stay **a few years** at the office, then go.
I'd rather put effort into **something with my hands**.
do: Stay **two or three years** at the office and save hard.
S3.quote: I'd rather put the effort into something with my hands.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **keep the wedding** on track for next September.
She'd still **refuse the tools**, preferring to unlearn nothing.
The **owned house** makes children feel possible even in this world.

steps.text: Stay at the benefits office two or three years and save hard
Take a furniture-finishing course before joining the workshop
Marry next September at St Mary's as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's be sensible. Don't rush. Let the people who like computers have the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the job's safe for a while and I'd keep it. I'd still not use the tools unless I had to. But I'd know it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at the office, marry Mark, maybe have a baby in three or four years. Around year six or seven I'd start working at the workshop. Keep the savings building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a slow way. It's a long way off, but I'd know the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd have time to raise a little one before it changes. I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My faith. Whatever happens, you have your family and your church. That doesn't change.

say: There's time, so **be sensible** and don't rush into anything.
Let the people who **like computers** have the computers.
think: The job's **safe for a while** and I'd keep it.
I'd still **not use the tools** unless I had to.
do: **Marry Mark** and maybe have a baby.
Move to the **workshop** around year six or seven.
S4.quote: Whatever happens, you have your family and your church.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **raise a child** before the change reaches her.
**Faith and family** are her anchors in every scenario.
She'd still keep **away from AI** while the job lasts.

steps.text: Marry Mark and plan a baby within four years
Keep working on the hardship fund desk without AI
Keep building the savings every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. There'd be no time to plan a family or a new trade. What would help is the government making sure there's still a person at the benefits office, and apprenticeships for people moving into hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about community. A market town runs on people knowing each other. If the benefits office becomes a website, nobody knows who's struggling anymore.

headlineQuote: If the benefits office becomes a website, nobody knows who's struggling anymore.
portrait: A **27-year-old hardship fund caseworker** in a market town, junior and slow on the rules.
She has **never used AI** and is pleased when the hype fails.
No rent and **good savings** make her secure, but her job is thinking work.
She turns to her **fiancé's joinery workshop** and family as AGI comes closer.
With ten years she'd **marry, have a child** and then switch to hands-on work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to plan a family or a trade.
whatWouldHelp: **A person** kept at every benefits office.
**Apprenticeships** for people moving into hands-on work.
